newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: Speculators seen targetting Malaysian ringgit next.
newsitem.headline: Speculators seen targetting Malaysian ringgit next.

text.p: The Malaysian ringgit is likely to be the next target of currency speculators after they successfully forced two central banks in the region to devalue their currencies, analysts said on Friday.
But they said Malaysia's central bank would put up a tough fight.

Bank Negara has itself warned would be aggressive in its efforts to stamp out speculation in the ringgit. It is backed by economic fundamentals widely regarded as stronger than most other countries in the region.
Analysts said the failure of the Thai and Philippine central banks to defend their currencies could lead to greater pressures on the Malaysian currency.
The Philippine central bank said on Friday it would allow the peso to trade in a wider range against the U.S. dollar, with immediate effect.
Dealers saw the move as the second de facto devaluation of an Asian currency in less than two weeks. The move came nine days after Thailand's decision to stage a managed float float of the baht.
The Philippine move sent Southeast Asian currencies into a tailspin on Friday. At 0600 GMT, the ringgit was quoted at 2.5020/30 to a dollar after opening around 2.4930.
"The bet is on that the ringgit will be the next currency to fall prey to speculators," said Sani Hamid, market analyst at research house MMS International in Singapore.
"But Bank Negara will do all it can to defend the ringgit. They can also impose capital controls as a last resort," he added.
Bank Negara governor Ahmad Mohamed Don on Wednesday warned of tough steps, including increasing interest rates, to curb speculation in the ringgit.
On Tuesday, Bank Negara intervened aggressively in the foreign exchange market, spending an estimated $1.0 billion to help the ringgit.
Ahmad said the intervention was warranted in the interest of long-term stability, adding that the central bank had sufficient reserves to fund such interventions.

Analysts said speculators are betting that Bank Negara will not be able to sustain its dollar/ringgit interventions as reserves are drawn down. But some believe Malaysia has sufficient reserves to defend its currency.
Bank Negara's reserves at the end of June stood at 70.71 billion ringgit ($28.3 billion).

"That provides substantially more ammunition than is available to the Philippine central bank which had about $11.5 billion at the beginning of the pressure, and was down to about $10 billion yesterday," said P.K. Basu, director of regional economics at UBS Securities.
"I don't see the ringgit succumbing to the pressures emanating from the currency market," he said.

Analysts said speculators are also betting that Bank Negara would not revert to capital controls as this would prove a major setback to Kuala Lumpur's goal of becoming an internationally recognised capital market.

In 1994, faced with a strong flow of hot money into the country, Bank Negara imposed negative interest rates on foreign deposits, banned swaps and stopped foreigners from buying Malaysian government paper.
Analysts said a ringgit devaluation was also unlikely.

"I don't see the real justification for it," said Nathan Balakrishnan, general manager at SBB Unit Trust Management. "Some are trying to short the ringgit because they think sentiment might affect the ringgit, but not fundamentally. Fundamentally I think we are better than Thailand and the Philippines," he said.
Unlike Thailand and Philippines, Malaysia's current account deficit is funded by long-term inflows.
In addition, Malaysia is the only economy in the region which has been able to maintain a strong economic growth, having posted growth of more than eight percent a year in the past nine years.
Unlike the baht and peso, the ringgit has been a free-floating currency since 1971.

"I would emphasise that Malaysia has always had a flexible currency regime ... over the past one year, the ringgit has fluctuated about 2.5 percent above and below the dollar. In the past 10 years, it has moved 10 percent either side," said Basu.
